title: Emergence of Correlations Between Records and Maximum in Random Time Series
authors: Satya N. Majumdar, Sanjib Sabhapandit, Gregory Schehr
abstract: We compute exactly the covariance between the maximum $M$ and the number of records $K$ in a discrete time series of $n$ entries as a quantitative probe of the history leading to an extreme event. For continuous IID series, with a common probability distribution function (PDF) $p(x)$, we find the striking result that $M$ and $K$ are uncorrelated for any $n \geq 1$. We show that this independence is rather fragile and the covariance $C_q(n)$ between $M$ and $K$ becomes nonzero when $p(x)$ becomes discontinuous due to a delta-component at $x=0$ with an amplitude $0< q < 1$. This time series models the occurrence of dry days with probability $q$ in a precipitation time series when there is no rainfall. We show that there is an interesting shape transition at a critical value $q_c$ where the covariance $C_q(n)$, as a function of $n$, changes from monotonic ($q<q_c$) to non monotonic behavior (for $q>q_c$). We compute the critical strength $q_c$ exactly. Furthermore, for large $n$, we show that $C_q(n)$ decays as a power law, with an exponent that depends on the tail of $p(x)$. We then compare our theoretical predictions with real precipitation data from several weather stations across Germany, finding a very good agreement.
summary: This work analyzes the correlation between the maximum value and the number of records in a random time series, using this as a probe for extreme events. By modeling precipitation data with 'dry days,' the authors show that correlations emerge when the underlying distribution is non-continuous. They precisely locate a critical threshold $q_c$ that dictates whether the correlation decays monotonically or exhibits a non-monotonic shape, validating these findings against real weather data.
main_problem: The paper computes the covariance between the global maximum ($M$) and the number of records ($K$) in a random time series to probe the history leading to extreme events.
main_result: The covariance is zero for continuous IID series but becomes non-zero when the distribution has a delta-component (modeling dry days), exhibiting a shape transition at a critical probability $q_c$.
method: The authors derive and analyze the joint Probability Generating Function (GF) for $K$ and $M$, calculating the covariance $C_q(n)$ both analytically and by comparing theory to empirical weather data.
model_or_system: The model is a discrete time series of $n$ entries, initially IID, but specialized to model precipitation data by introducing a probability $q$ for a 'dry day' (value 0), creating a non-continuous PDF.
key_observables: Covariance $C_q(n) = \langle MK angle - \langle M angle \langle K angle$, Global Maximum ($M$), Number of Records ($K$).
important_parameters: The dry-day probability $q$, the critical threshold $q_c$, and the tail behavior of the underlying continuous PDF $f(x)$.
main_assumptions: The entries $X_i$ are assumed to be IID, although the analysis extends to non-IID structures via the delta-component.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the theoretical shape transition of $C_q(n)$ versus $n$ at $q_c$, and show a very good agreement between the theoretical predictions and real German precipitation data.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the uncorrelated nature of $M$ and $K$ for continuous data. It then introduces the dry-day model ($q>0$), deriving the joint GF and showing the emergence of $C_q(n)$. The core analysis focuses on the shape transition at $q_c$ and the asymptotic power-law decay, concluding with comparisons to empirical weather records.
why_interesting: While the topic is classical time series analysis, the rigorous mathematical framework for calculating correlations in extreme value statistics and the connection to physical processes (like dry spells) touches upon non-equilibrium statistical mechanics and fluctuation analysis.
